title: High oil prices have led to a dip in global carbon emissions
author: Scott K. Johnson
body: Evaluating the annual global temperatures each year requires context. There is a fair amount of natural variability from one year to the next, so it’s important to focus on the trend over time. Famously, global warming did not end in 1998, as some claimed a couple of decades ago—we just had a run of La-Niña-dominated years after a very strong El Niño. Annual greenhouse gas emissions are much less variable, having increased fairly steadily, but many complicating factors can still muddy the picture. Sometimes those factors conspire to throw a year off the trend. It looks like 2026 will be one of those years. A new analysis led by Corinne Le Quéré at the University of East Anglia estimates that fossil fuel emissions have fallen about 0.4 percent from last year. This probably isn’t a peak that symbolizes heartening progress on climate change, though; the researchers think it’s a short-term dip driven by the war in Iran and its effect on oil prices. title: One space station company sues another for copying its work
author: Eric Berger
body: NASA's competition for the development of private space stations that will take flight in the 2030s is already nearing crunch time. But a recently unsealed lawsuit may spice things up even further. The lawsuit involves two of the most prominent companies in this competition, Houston-based Axiom Space and Long Beach, California-based Vast Space. And it is surfacing as final proposals for private space stations are due from companies to the US space agency a little more than one month from today, on December 14 . According to the court filings unsealed by a November 4 order from US District Judge Charles Eskridge, Axiom is pursuing a False Claims Act case against Vast in which Axiom accuses Vast of presenting NASA with a fraudulent mission-planning document that incorporates Axiom's proprietary information. title: GTA 6 on PS5 vs. Xbox: What we know
body: Grand Theft Auto VI is less than two weeks away, which means it's time to sort out which console you're going to play it on at launch, if you haven't already. The problem there is that Rockstar Games has given us precious little information to go on regarding how the game looks and runs on PS5 versus the Xbox Series consoles. The official marketing spin has been that GTA 6 "plays best" on PS5 for months now, but Rockstar had not greatly expanded on what that means...until now. SEE ALSO: How to play 'GTA 6' a day before everyone else in the U.S. GTA 6 on PS5 and PS5 Pro: What to expect In a statement that coincided with the game becoming available for pre-load on Tuesday, Rockstar elaborated a little bit on what to expect from each console version of the game, while also sharing a new 30-second trailer. According to Rockstar, GTA6 will target 30 frames per second on every machine at launch, which is not a surprise given the level of visual fidelity on display. Rockstar also said the PS5 Pro version will support PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), a special technique the PS5 Pro uses to enhance game resolution. Beyond that, PS5 Pro users will have access to ray-traced shadows, meaning (presumably) that every shadow in the game will react realistically to light sources. No other console version of the game will support this feature, at least not at launch. We've already seen the base PS5 version running in the big Netflix trailer back in August, but Rockstar elaborated a bit on that version, too. title: DeepMind reveals Gemini Robotics 2.5 and open safety benchmark "ASIMOV-jailbreak"
author: Ryan Whitwam
body: Google DeepMind has revealed a new generation of the AI-powered Gemini Robotics platform. In the 2.5 release, Google says its robotic AI is getting tantalizingly close to completing real-world tasks as well as humans do. In fact, some Gemini robots were able to get actual work done in Mercedes-Benz factories, and the team is preparing for a day when robots operate alongside humans with an open source safety benchmark. DeepMind's physical AI platform has several computational layers between user input and robotic action. There's the vision-language model piece, which is Gemini Embodied Reasoning. Essentially, it takes your instructions and uses live video to plan how the robot can accomplish the task. The other main component is the vision-language-action (VLA) that actually generates robot actions, like moving an actuator—that's Gemini Robotics, which has been bumped to version 2.5. DeepMind says that Gemini Robotics 2.5 is much better at tasks that require a high degree of dexterity. The model was evaluated across more than 200 activities, including serving food with tongs and using a pipette, as you would see in a laboratory. Google also showed that Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot with Gemini Robotics 2.5 can now tie a bow with its five-fingered hands, a notable feat, because deformable objects (like ribbon) are notoriously difficult for robots to manipulate. title: FDA warns GLP-1 drugs may pose risk of rare condition that causes vision loss
author: Beth Mole
body: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that popular obesity drugs—including Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound, and Mounjaro—may carry a "potential increased risk" of a rare eye condition that can lead to permanent vision loss. In a drug safety communication Monday , the FDA said it will now require makers of GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs to add a warning about that risk on their drug labels. The specific eye condition it warns of is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or NAION . The condition is caused by restricted blood flow to the optic nerve, which leads to swelling and cell death and ultimately damages the nerve, causing abrupt vision loss that can often be permanent. It's unknown how GLP-1 drugs may cause NAION. The condition is rare overall, occurring in somewhere between two and 10 people in 100,000 in the general population, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmologists. These small numbers have made it more difficult to determine with certainty if there is a connection. Further complicating the potential link is the fact that the risk factors for developing NAION are common among patients taking GLP-1 drugs. The risk factors include diabetes, cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, metabolic syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea. Read full article Comments

title: Apples new iOS 27.2.1 fixes critical bugs, and you should install it now
body: Apple 's new iOS 27.2.1, released on Monday, doesn't bring any new features, but that doesn't mean you should sleep on it. In fact, you should install it right away, as it includes patches for numerous bugs, including some critical software vulnerabilities. SEE ALSO: Apple might turn Siri AI into an agent next year Apple's official release notes for this release (alongside iPadOS, which was also updated to version 27.2.1) highlight nine separate bugs, including one in which an app could be used to access sensitive user data, one in which an attacker could pair with a user's device without user interaction, and one in which a remote attacker could be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. One particularly nasty bug was highlighted on Tuesday by cryptocurrency exchange Binance, which infamously had a massive security breach in late October . "A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance," wrote Binance in a tweet, urging users to delete apps installed from untrusted sources, and to update iOS and all apps to the latest official versions. This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed. Apple's iOS 27.2.1 is available to iOS users through Settings - General - Software Update. title: Polestar has a new look with its Formula 2030 concept
author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
body: Perhaps only a small percentage of Ars readers will care about the Polestar 2030 concept, debuted today by the electric automaker. Spun out of Volvo—once upon a time, Polestar was a racing team—the brand has leveraged the resources of parent-automaker Geely to create electric vehicles that marry a modern minimalist style with rewarding driving dynamics . But you now can’t buy any Polestars in the US , since Geely is Chinese, and banning Chinese-owned car brands enjoys remarkable bipartisan support in Congress. The Formula 2030 is about the same length as a Polestar 2 but with a very low roofline. If anything, the two-box shape reminds me of the Saab Aero-X, one of the final concepts from the then-terminal Swedish automaker. (In many ways, Polestar has adopted Saab’s mantle.) Credit: Polestar These rear lights will show up in production Polestars. In 2008, Saab showed off the Aero-X concept. Credit: Scott Barbour/Getty Images Polestar says the concept fits into its own segment somewhere between the next Polestar 2 and the Polestar 7—it numbers its cars chronologically (mostly), not based on size—although it’s not saying if the hatchback form factor will go into series production. Successfully packaging the rear seat passengers and a lithium-ion battery pack is something a concept needn’t worry about, after all. Rather, it’s a styling exercise, or more than one. title: Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
author: Jeremy Hsu
body: Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting. Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones. Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. The finished spools can hold enough fiber-optic cable for drones to regularly operate at ranges of dozens of miles, and sometimes up to 62 miles (100 kilometers) in extreme cases, as reported by the independent Russian publication The Insider . title: Review: Apple's M6 MacBook Pro is good, but it's missing all the exciting stuff
author: Andrew Cunningham
body: I've written more than once about the weird positioning of Apple's entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro, which has always occupied an uncomfortable perch between the MacBook Air and the higher-end MacBook Pros. The best versions of this laptop, like last year's M5 refresh, come with the same basic design and external features of the higher-end MacBook Pros, just with a more modest processor and a lower ceiling for specs like RAM and storage. The lesser versions stick with older designs or other compromises, reserving Apple's most updated designs and screen technologies for the more expensive high-end models. Recall the 13-inch M1 and M2 MacBook Pros, which stuck with Apple's 2016-era MacBook Pro designs for everything , up to and including the now-abandoned Touch Bar. (If you're someone at Apple maintaining Touch Bar support into the 2030s for the sake of these two laptop models, I'd like to hear from you. Not for a story! I'd just like to know how you are.) This year's entry-level MacBook Pro mostly falls into that latter category. It does get an Apple M6 chip, and the M6 is great—rumors suggest the M6 won't get Pro, Max, or Ultra configurations, so there are some fringe benefits here that you can't get in the top-tier MacBook Pros. But it uses the same MacBook Pro design Apple has been using since 2021 . There's no touchscreen, no OLED panel, no Dynamic Island, no half-pound weight reduction, no glowing Apple logo on the lid. title: What is Muse Ember? Meet Meta’s new low-cost AI model
body: Booking a vacation sounds like one thing to hand off to an AI assistant, right up until it has to check the calendar, open a dozen tabs, and figure out whether the cheapest flight is still the cheapest once a carry-on is involved. Every one of those steps takes work, and when an AI agent is doing it, the cost can add up. Meta has a new model built for that part of the job. On Nov. 9, Meta's Superintelligence Labs introduced Muse Ember , which the company calls its smallest and most cost-efficient AI model yet. It's designed for the steps an agent might repeat dozens of times in a single assignment, like pulling details out of a document, calling another tool, or running a test after changing a line of code. Muse is the app with the cute little avatar named Jolly that Meta has been promoting since September. The AI assistant can work across (some) apps with a user's permission. The app passed 5 million downloads in 22 days , and has already had many updates; last week, Meta started rolling out voice conversations and animated avatars for the assistant in the U.S. Meta also uses the Muse name for a family of AI models. The company positions Muse Wonder as the model for its toughest problems and Muse Spark as a model for coding and other work that involves using tools. Ember is the cheaper option for repeatable tasks. Meta's pitch is that developers can use Wonder to plan a complicated job and hand off the individual steps to Ember. For now, Meta lists Ember as available through its Muse Code tool and developer API . SEE ALSO: Meta launches Muse Wonder, catching OpenAI and Ant

title: Mediums new app tries to save the platform from irrelevance
body: A personal essay, a tutorial, or an argument that's been knocking around in someone's head for weeks can all find a home on Medium. Now the platform wants to be part of what happens before those pieces are ready to publish when a writer is still sorting through notes or sending an early draft to a friend. On Nov. 9, Medium launched TK , a free writing and note-taking app for people with a Medium account. TK has an AI assistant built into the editor that can answer questions or give feedback as writers draft. It also lets writers share work in small groups where others can leave comments, swap notes, or contribute writing of their own. It's goal, according to CEO of Medium Tony Stubblebine, is to "craft writing that compounds into deep thinking, which creates influence across your entire world. What shape is that influence? We re still figuring that out, but we know it starts with humans writing more." "We ve designed TK for three goals: Easy to write. Easy to think. Easy to feel like your writing matters," he added. The launch comes as the internet has changed. Medium relies on Google to send readers to its articles ( 44 percent of their traffic, specifically ), and Stubblebine said those referrals declined "When Google started taking away all the traffic." He warned the company in an interview with The Verge that "this hurts us, but it also hurts you." Though Medium is profitable since 2024 , iterating must be done to compete with both other publishing platforms (like Substack ) and social media. body: The leather-jacketed CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, spurring an investigation by his company and intense discussions worldwide. Recent reporting noted that since last year, US intelligence reports had identified Alice Huang (no relation) as not only the exec for an AI compute company renting access to Nvidia GPUs, but also a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies, including the “neoclouds” like Coreweave who have been some of its biggest customers. So far, Nvidia and Jensen Huang have said that they have “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that hasn’t settled things as the investigation continues. title: A transitioning Congress finds itself in a pickle on AI data centers
body: As Congress returns to Washington this week, the massive power demands of the AI boom have forced a reckoning over data center infrastructure. The Senate is preparing for a pivotal procedural vote on legislation that would speed approvals for energy projects while requiring large data centers to shoulder more of the costs they impose on the power grid. The bipartisan bill would add much-needed regulations on data centers, but, as some politicians believe , may also encourage more data center construction. Silicon Valley vs. a changed D.C. In the sweeping and history-making midterm elections last week, voters didn't just elect a new generation of Democratic lawmakers. They also sent a pretty unmistakable message to Big Tech, particularly the artificial intelligence industry: Enough with the data centers already. Or, more bluntly, "get out of town." Across the country, local communities are pushing to stop, restrict, or impose conditions on data center development. The election results reinforced that message, making clear that the AI gold rush is facing growing resistance. For the last two years, Silicon Valley has busied itself building more, building bigger and doing it ASAP. If a tech giant wanted to drop a warehouse-sized data center into a community, local governments often offered tax breaks and other incentives, then told residents it was harmless and would mean more jobs. We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. title: The blue wave has caused ripples of hetero-optimism
body: On Nov. 3, left-leaning Americans felt something that had lain dormant for a long time: hope. The U.S. midterm elections resulted in historic wins , including Democrats flipping seats in several states. After the gut-punch of Trump's second win in 2024, and the subsequent human rights abuses and skyrocketing costs in the last two years, the "blue wave" (or bluenami, bluke, however you'd like to refer to it) swept over many of us like a calming balm. SEE ALSO: Midterms deliver clear message: 'The AI reckoning is here' The election results haven't just caused democratic optimism (or millennial optimism ). For some women who date men, it has also bubbled over into romantic optimism. "I'm hopeful that with a shift in politics and culture, the values of individuals and groups will start to shift too," Bailey Cummings, a 27-year-old communications and marketing specialist based in Nashville, told Mashable over Instagram DM. Is heteropessimism fading? The past few years have been less than stellar for heterosexuals. In 2019, writer and researcher Asa Seresin coined " heteropessimism ," or feelings of shame, regret, and hopelessness when it comes to straight romance. The feeling seems to have only gotten worse since then, paving the way for 2025's " heterofatalism ." The novelty of dating apps has long worn off, the debate over whether to engage in casual sex rages on, and having a boyfriend is embarrassing . title: What is code rot? How a software term became TikTok slang.
body: An old video game can look just the way it did years ago, right up until a door that used to open won't budge, a character stops responding when you try to talk to them, or the game freezes every time you load a saved level. That's one way to run into what programmers call "code rot. " The game itself may have stayed the same while the platform it runs on keeps getting updates. Over time, parts of the game stop working altogether. On Gen Z TikTok, anything can be "code rotted," from a report card full of failing grades to a slushie machine that won t dispense the goods. The joke is that real life is starting to break down like an old Roblox game , especially when something that's supposed to go right just doesn't. Creators write text overlays in the voice of someone who's just confirmed a long-held suspicion: A baffling homework assignment? "Yup yup yup i f*cking knew it this assignment is definitely code rotted." Can't log into your Google account? "google is coderotted. it's coderot." Puppy acting up? It's code-rotted, too . title: A Sam Altman parody offers an amusing lesson in memory management
author: Nick Indge
body: Sam Altman's recent comments on the Cheeky Pint podcast inspired developer Iain Kay to create a satirical script that allows users to email the OpenAI CEO once per day if more than 10 percent of their system RAM is reported as available. Ram-Altman is described by its creator as a "parody project" launched in response to Altman's viral remarks about RAM in your personal PC. As reported by The Verge , on the October 29 episode recorded with Stripe President John Collison, Altman said, "A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center. But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5 percent of the time." Altman has since explained that his comments were taken out of context and briefly changed his display name to "RAM Altman" on X, which Kay calls on the project GitHub, "objectively excellent and where the project gets its name." title: Jensen Huang Nvidia affair scandal: What we know, what we don’t
body: On Sunday, chipmaker Nvidia posted an odd press release from its founder and CEO Jensen Huang on its website's newsroom page. The press release, titled "A Message to Our Company," was also emailed to the company's employees. "I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Why did Huang, who leads one of the most valuable companies in the world, share this personal information through official corporate communications? It's because the woman he had an affair with has been accused of working as a spy for China, according to reports from the New York Times and the Financial Times . And this goes beyond just a public relations scandal. With Huang being a leading figure in the AI industry, Nvidia being the major supplier of computing power for the AI boom, and the AI arms race between the U.S. and China, Huang's affair is also an issue of national security. What we know The New York Times and the Financial Times reported over the weekend that Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese citizen and top executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, a major purchaser of Nvidia's chips. According to the outlets, U.S. intelligence agencies believe that Alice Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security as a spy. title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
author: Dan Goodin
body: Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting. The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real. Attackers conducting "mature intrusions" Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI. Read full article Comments

title: Pentagon mulls placing fleet of military satellites around the Moon
author: Stephen Clark
body: The US military has published a Request for Information on a federal procurement website signaling interest in deploying a "proliferated cislunar constellation" consisting of an unspecified number of satellites performing an undisclosed mission in the vicinity of the Moon. The announcement follows statements in recent months from the Space Force's acquisitions chief for advanced programs, Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy, that the military was getting serious about extending its reach to the Moon. The Space Force's most distant satellites today are in geostationary orbit, some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) over the equator, collecting routine surveillance and missile warning data. Most recently, Purdy spoke of a shift in Pentagon leadership's thinking about the Moon following an executive order signed by President Donald Trump last December. The order set out the Trump administration's space policy. One section of the order deals with the US government's ability to detect, characterize, and counter threats to US space interests from low-Earth orbit to cislunar space, the term of art for the region of space around the Moon. title: Raanan Hershberg on Stand-Up, Beating the Algorithm & Finding Your Voice
body: Raanan Hershberg is a comic s comic, known for sharp, long-form premises, ruthless self-awareness, and a distinct refusal to bend entirely to the internet s whims. Over years grinding through the New York stand-up scene, making specials like Brave and Jokes from the Underground , and co-hosting Your Favorite Movie Sucks , he has built a reputation for comedy that digs into the messy, uncomfortable gray areas of modern life. In this in-depth conversation, Hershberg sits down to discuss the development of his latest hour, Did You Like Me? , the modern reality of social media virality, and why protecting your artistic integrity matters more than ever. In this episode, Hershberg takes a sobering look back at early 2000s "punching-down" material, the guilt of edgy comedy, and turning domestic arguments into sharper, honest material. Hershberg then dives into the illusion of truth in stand-up, why audiences naturally suspend disbelief, how breaking the fourth wall creates bigger laughs, and the art of admitting when a joke is a lie. Hershberg also addresses the dreaded algorithm trap: why chasing short viral clips compromises a comic s voice, the line between smart promotion and writing for social media, and why virality often comes from people completely misunderstanding the joke. Catch Raanan Hershberg performing his hour Did You Like Me? live at the 2026 New York Comedy Festival and watch his specials including his award-winning short film Memory Room available now on YouTube. title: The Ocarina of Time remake is setting Metacritic records left and right
body: Nintendo appears to have made the right call in remaking The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 , at least from a hearts-and-minds perspective. The visually resplendent remake, which hit store shelves last week, has already set two records on Metacritic in just a few days. For starters, it has the highest aggregate score (96 out of 100) of any game to be released in 2026 so far . That was established when reviews went up a week ago, though, so it's not necessarily news at this point. However, as Forbes noted, Ocarina for Switch 2 has achieved another gaudy Metacritic milestone: It's now the highest-rated game by user scores in the site's history, with an all-time record score of 9.6 out of 10. SEE ALSO: 6 good, bad, and weird changes in 'The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 For reference, the original Ocarina of Time for Nintendo 64 is the highest-rated game by critics in the history of Metacritic, with a score of 99 out of 100, a record it's held for a long time. More than 8,750 users have submitted scores for Ocarina on Metacritic, so that score isn't necessarily being affected by a small sample size. It should absolutely be noted and emphasized that Metacritic does not require a verification of purchase for a user to submit a review score, so it's theoretically possible that some people are adding numbers to the mix in either direction without having played the game. title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
author: Kyle Orland
body: Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That's the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets , including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories. The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the "Yes, and don't ask again" option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local ".claude/settings.local.json" file on the user's computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it. This isn't really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user's local machine (assuming that machine doesn't become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer's global .gitignore list , which usually prevents it from being shared publicly. title: SpaceX now fundamentally an "infrastructure company," senior official says
author: Eric Berger
body: For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with the development of newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence. At last week's UP.Summit conference in Florida, the vice president of launch at SpaceX, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company's changing focus, how it is embracing AI, and why the Falcon 9 rocket—which has dominated global launch for a decade and remains the world's preeminent launch vehicle—is firmly on the road to retirement. "In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point," Dontchev said. "We're building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars." Read full article Comments

title: F1 in Brazil: You’ve got to keep your tires alive
author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
body: In sports, a “ dead rubber ” is a match that takes place after the outcome of the series or championship has already been decided. The people in charge hate this*—if you wrap up a title two-thirds of the way through a season, the viewers evaporate, as there’s nothing left at stake. But anyone who decided to skip this year’s Brazilian Grand Prix this past weekend missed one of the year’s most entertaining races, as a combination of a mixed-up starting order, some very fast drivers at the back, and a wet track that dried and then saw rain again resulted in action aplenty. A peculiarity of F1 is that even if you manage to win a championship, there’s no guarantee you’ll be in a position to defend it. Take McLaren’s Lando Norris, who took the crown in 2025 after a nail-biting fight with his teammate Oscar Piastri and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Sadly for Lando, McLaren did not start this year in a position to win races, and even with several upgrades, the team has produced a car that is still very tricky to drive. But this weekend in Brazil, Norris demonstrated the form that earned him the number 1. Rain on Saturday during qualifying helped jumble the usual running order. It was heavy enough that drivers used the wet weather tire with deep treads, which usually generates so much spray that visibility disappears and running has to be suspended. But with fewer cars on track in the later knockout qualifying sessions, this was not a problem for once. title: Elon Musk insists Cybertruck demand is strong as Tesla scraps it
body: Tesla Cybertruck is dead. The massive, steel-plated electric pickup has never sold particularly well, and Tesla CEO Elon Musk said last week that Cybertruck production will wind down next year. Musk would like the world to know, however, that the company isn't scrapping Cybertruck due to unprofitability or lack of demand. This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed. "The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people," wrote Musk in a tweet on Monday. "This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media, but rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production," he wrote. That's an interesting logical hoop Musk would like you to jump through. Given that Tesla doesn't report precise Cybertruck sales numbers, and typically doesn't talk about profitability of individual models, it's hard for an outsider to definitively call this or that model unprofitable. We've never said it, by the way; we merely pointed to poor sales figures, based on reports and Tesla's own figures, which lump Cybertruck with "other models" in quarterly reports . But how do we know the sales figures are bad? Well, we merely compare Musk's predictions with actual sales numbers. title: Xfinity introduces WiFi-pausing Holiday Mode feature, with help from John C. Reilly
body: Xfinity is introducing a new "Holiday Mode" feature in its app, with a little help from actor John C. Reilly , who plays the Ghost of Very-Recent Christmas Past in a new holiday advertisement. Holiday Mode lets customers pause WiFi for all devices on their home network with a single tap on their phone screen. The idea is to keep families connected and off their phones, if only for a few precious moments during the holidays. The company said that Holiday Mode will be available starting from Nov. 9 for eligible Xfinity Internet customers through the Xfinity app. The company also debuted a new Christmas advertisement to promote the feature, starring the aforementioned ghost. Reilly's character rescues people who miss precious holiday moments because they can't look away from their phones, an unfortunately relatable scenario. 90-second and 60-second versions of the holiday ad are debuting on Nov. 9 on YouTube and TV. Our business is built around keeping people connected, so telling families to turn off their WiFi might seem like an unexpected move," said Julie Scelzo, the Chief Creative Officer of Xfinity at Comcast, in a press release shared with Mashable. "But at Xfinity, we believe that sometimes the most important connections happen IRL. And at the holidays, stepping away from our screens makes room for the wonder of time spent together. Technology should enhance our lives, not get in the way of it." The Ghost of Very-Recent Christmas Past Credit: Xfinity If you're an Xfinity Internet customer, here's how to activate Holiday Mode: Open the Xfinity app and select Holiday Mod

title: New Democratic Congress will likely strip the gilding from Trump's Golden Dome
author: Stephen Clark
body: Two of the top lawmakers backing the Pentagon's Golden Dome missile defense shield are among the wave of Republicans leaving Congress in the coming Democratic takeover, raising questions about the future of President Donald Trump's signature second-term defense initiative. The shakeup on Capitol Hill comes after military officials signaled in recent months that they might backpedal from one element Trump asked for in Golden Dome: the capability to shoot down missiles in their initial boost phase shortly after launch. The Golden Dome has escaped serious congressional scrutiny since Trump announced the program in January 2025, one week into his second term in the White House. That lack of scrutiny will change as Democrats take responsibility for writing the Pentagon's budget, introduce limits on funding, and put forth bills to strip out Golden Dome's most controversial component and give the program a new name. title: Meta announces global roll out of its age estimation system
body: Meta announced Monday that it will roll out its age-estimation technology globally. The move puts millions more teens around the world into Teen Accounts settings on Instagram, the company said in a blog post . In April 2025, Meta began using AI technology to detect teens on Instagram, even if they'd used an adult age upon opening an account. Once identified, teens are proactively put into Meta's safest settings, which are designed to limit inappropriate content. This month, parents in the U.S. will begin seeing a video in their Instagram feed explaining how teens are placed in age-appropriate protections. SEE ALSO: European Commission advises TikTok to redesign FYP or risk fines "We ll continue to do our part to proactively ensure teens are in age-appropriate experiences on our apps," the blog post said. Still, Meta has spent the year under fire for its ability to protect young users. In March, the company lost a case brought by the state of New Mexico , which alleged that Meta's design features helped pedophiles sexually exploit children on Meta platforms. A jury found Meta liable for misleading consumers about endangering children and the safety of its platforms. Meta, which said it would fight the decision, was ordered to pay nearly $950 billion in related penalties . In August, Meta made a $12 billion settlement with dozens of state attorneys general in a trial over whether the social media company had designed addictive platforms. title: Want to live and work on the moon? NASA is hiring.
body: Ever looked at the moon and thought, man, I'd love to work there? Well, NASA is hiring. Announced over the weekend, applications are now open for the next batch of astronauts who will train specifically to work and live on the lunar surface. SEE ALSO: Artemis II crew witnessed meteor flashes on the moon with their own eyes The U.S. space agency is looking for the next class to be trained at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, those "who will join NASA as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base, and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars." Applications close 11:59 p.m. ET Dec. 3 and NASA will make its selections in late 2027. Saturday's announcement came with a "NASA wants you" recruitment video, featuring NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Andre Douglas, Deniz Burnham, Randy Bresnik, Kayla Barron, Jack Hathaway, and Chris Williams. Notably, remote work isn't available for astronauts, and relocation fees to Houston may be covered by NASA. But the salary is out of this world: between $164,395 to $164,395 per year. Of course, you can't just spacewalk into a job on the moon. To apply , you'll need to be a U.S. citizen with a master's degree in a STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) field from an accredited institution. If you don't have the latter, NASA will also accept currently enrolled or completed Test Pilot School students (who also have a STEM bachelor's degree), people with medical degrees with professional experience or completed residency training, or people who have completed two years of a STEM-based doctoral program. title: Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 9, 2026
body: There's barely any of the Moon visible tonight as it approaches the New Moon. With less than a sliver illuminated, there is nothing for us to see in the way of lunar features. What is today's Moon phase? As of Monday, Nov. 9, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the New Moon phase, with 0% of its surface visible. When is the next Full Moon? The next Full Moon will take place on November 24. What are Moon phases? It takes the Moon around 29.5 days to pass through a complete lunar cycle. As it travels around Earth, the angle at which sunlight reaches its surface changes what we can see from here, producing the different phases, from the New Moon through to the Full Moon and back again. The cycle then starts over, as explained by NASA . The eight phases are: New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye). Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere). First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon. Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet. Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible. Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere) Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit. Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

title: Steps review: Cinderellas story with a goth girl twist (plus, a hot troll!)
body: In 2025, The Ugly Stepsister was one of our favorite horror movies of the year , reimagining the Cinderella princess tale as a critique of the extreme lengths girls are pressured to go to be beautiful. But if that sounds a bit intense for you (or your kiddos), Netflix has a less savage spin on this story. Steps also imagines how this story of fairy godmothers and glass slippers played out for the maligned stepsisters. And honestly, it's more charming than any of these princes. Aimed squarely at being family-friendly, Steps leans on the Disney and DreamWorks movies that have come before to tell a story that feels familiar yet fresh. Like classic Disney princess stories, there's a picture-perfect maiden in Cinderella, who is kind, cheerful, and talks to animals when she's not singing to villagers. But like Shrek, Steps opens with a classic storybook hinting at the familiar fairy tale, then has a snarky protagonist step into frame who's tired of being misrepresented. In this case, it's no ogre but a so-called "Evil Stepsister." And sure, Lilith (voiced by Ali Wong) is kind of mean to the orphaned Cinderella. She did technically order her to clean the fireplace. And she scorned Cinderella s animal friends. Plus, she tore up the dress that Cinderella had planned to wear to the prince's ball. But in context , these actions come off way less evil and way more teen angst. This is not a princess tale, but a story about misfits, alt fashion, sisterhood, and assimilation. And it's a joyously entertaining ride to boot! Steps offers a parable about being true to yourself. Lilith and Mar

title: Would you pay Spotify extra to remix your favorite songs with AI?
body: Spotify already uses AI to help pick what plays next. But its planned remix tool , reportedly set for release early next year, would let listeners change what they're hearing. How does it work? Let's say a slow breakup ballad comes on at a party. A subscriber could turn it into a dance track that better fits the vibe. Want a new artist's voice? The tool could also make a different singer cover the song, even if they've never recorded it before. Spotify first announced the tool in May, but it got people talking again on Oct. 30, when the Financial Times reported that the company was targeting an early 2027 launch and considering charging Premium subscribers an extra $4 to $5 a month. SEE ALSO: Spotify already has AI playlists. So what does Meta s Muse add? What subscribers would get for that extra fee depends on which musicians sign up in the first place. At this point, Spotify has deals with Universal Music Group, Merlin, Believe, and Kobalt, but the FT reported that artists would decide individually whether to participate, even if their label had signed a deal. Believe and TuneCore artists would first have to agree to be considered for AI projects, then decide separately whether to join Spotify's program. Some listeners are already talking about leaving The plan raises different questions for fans and musicians. For people who ve been paying for Spotify for years, the discussion quickly moved past whether they d buy the add-on to whether they wanted to keep their subscription at all. title: Is this the only U.S. town to vote yes on data centers?
body: On Election Day, voters approved more than 40 measures to slow or ban data center growth . But not all Americans decided against data centers. The majority of voters in Harwood, North Dakota, said "no" to a ballot measure calling for additional steps when the town evaluates, approves, and administers developments like that of data centers, Tech Insider reported. In a town of 845 people, 430 voted, and around 75 percent voted against added restrictions. (As Tech Insider notes, however, that documentation on small towns could be varied The Washington Post reports that Harwood's population is 845, while other outlets report 940.) SEE ALSO: Data center security is an American problem, too The big project in question is a $3 billion, 1.8-million-square-foot data center right outside Harwood , the Washington Post reports. Data center developer Applied Digital is behind the project. The vote caused the Post to claim that Harwood is "the only town in the U.S. that said yes to data centers." While the building of a data center itself wasn't on the ballot, Harwood residents indeed voted against further bureaucracy towards them. Harwood breaks the trend of what happened on Election Day, which Mashable's Rebecca Ruiz said was a clear message: " The AI reckoning is here ." Backlash to both AI and data centers had been mounting in 2026, and voters were able to express their discontent last Tuesday. The list of U.S. states that ban data centers could grow in 2027.

title: Druski brings out Emma Stone in historic SNL monologue
body: "Let s go!" Druski yelled as he walked onto the Studio 8H stage late Nov. 7. The comedian, who's spent years making people laugh on their phones, was the first digital content creator to host Saturday Night Live , with The Strokes as musical guest (which Druski does a spot-on impression of , by the way). How much of the comedy that got him there could he actually do on live TV? That was one of his first jokes. Druski, whose real name is Drew Desbordes, opened his monologue by assuring the audience that SNL wouldn't water down his comedy, though he said he'd been asked to skip the swearing and not dress in whiteface ( surprise, it didn't last very long ). By his count, there went about half his material. Anyone who's watched him play the boss of Coulda Been Records , a fictional label that holds chaotic auditions for aspiring artists, could see why he'd have a little trouble making that promise. Between those auditions and his dating show Coulda Been Love , Druski had amassed more than 6 million subscribers and nearly 2 billion views on YouTube. Credit: Screenshot: SNL on YouTube The comedian also joked that there might be some truth to the rumors that he was taking Ozempic, then took a moment to shout out his family in the audience where one family member shouted for "more money!" After reflecting on how much had happened over the past year, he asked the crowd how he could repay them. His answer was, apparently, to bring out Emma Stone. title: "Thats Senator Talafreako": James Talarico crashes SNL
body: After a week of surprise election results , one question remained heading into Saturday night: How would Saturday Night Live open its first show since the midterms? The Nov. 7 cold open started at a Democratic victory party, where Chuck Schumer (Sarah Sherman) and Hakeem Jeffries (Kenan Thompson) happily took credit for the party s wins. They were also excited about the younger Democrats headed to Congress...as long as nobody expected them to give up their jobs. Before the party could go much further, James Austin Johnson's Donald Trump cut in, interrupting the duo to discuss the election results a recurring bit in the SNL universe. Credit: Screenshot: SNL on YouTube Trump was impressed with himself for accepting the results and even put on a hard hat to talk about the White House ballroom , which was still what he cared about most, of course. But he was considerably less excited about working with millennials . He rattled off a few things he associated with the generation, including mason jar weddings and the sitcom New Girl , then got sidetracked explaining why he thought the show improved once Winston adopted a cat. In his view, giving Winston a pet finally gave the writers something to do with him. OK then? Trump eventually circled back to the millennials he'd have to work with. When he got to Texas senator-elect James Talarico, he called him "Talafreako," a real nickname the real Trump had used on the campaign trail. title: Tiny galaxies lose most of their oxygen. No one knows where it goes.
body: Let this sink into your chest: The oxygen in every breath you take formed inside stars. But new research from NASA 's Hubble Space Telescope shows small galaxies hurl away most of the oxygen their stars produce. Astronomers studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies , which hold anywhere from a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars. On average, those galaxies kept just 11 percent of the oxygen their stars made over time. The most efficient ones held onto about a quarter; the worst among them retained just 4 percent. Much larger galaxies tend to have three to four times as much, earlier studies have shown. Exploding stars likely drove the rest away. When massive stars die in blasts called supernovas , they unleash winds strong enough to push gas clear out of a galaxy. Dwarf galaxies have weak gravity, so they struggle to hold onto that material. Astronomers want to know where the oxygen that stars forge ends up, and how much of it a galaxy can store. A project called Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds, or GLOW, tracks that oxygen inside stars, through the gas between them, and out into the space between galaxies. Because oxygen outnumbers every element except hydrogen and helium, it makes a good tracer for how galaxies recycle matter broadly. Astronomers can measure it easily, and they know how stars make it. "So, it's really for practical reasons that we've chosen oxygen," said Kristen Wingfield McQuinn, GLOW principal investigator at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, in a statement . title: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
author: Jacek Krywko
body: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why. In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate. The missing electrons Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said. What is today's Moon phase? As of Sunday, Nov. 8, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waning Crescent phase, with 1% of its surface visible. Visibility it too low tonight, so you won't be able to see any lunar features. When is the next Full Moon? The next Full Moon will take place on November 24. What are Moon phases? It takes the Moon around 29.5 days to pass through a complete lunar cycle. As it travels around Earth, the angle at which sunlight reaches its surface changes what we can see from here, producing the different phases, from the New Moon through to the Full Moon and back again. The cycle then starts over, as explained by NASA . The eight phases are: New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye). Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere). First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon. Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet. Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible. Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere) Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit. Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

title: Chinas moon plan mirrors NASAs, except for one big difference
body: China's plan to land people on the moon by 2030 mirrors NASA 's on paper but skips crewed lunar test flights, trusting robotic rehearsals for its first human landing instead. Chinese space officials laid out their approach at the 7th Manned Space Symposium in Beijing on Oct. 31, according to Xinhua , the Chinese government's wire service. A slide reportedly from the presentation posted by CNSpaceflight, an independent outlet that tracks the Chinese space program, shows two of the initial missions with nobody aboard. A crew flies the Mengzhou, or "Dream Vessel," capsule to Earth orbit in 2027. Then the robots take over. The Lanyue, or "Embracing the Moon," lander touches down on its own in 2028, and an uncrewed mission rehearses the full landing sequence in 2029. "For any crewed mission, we will try to fly it in an unmanned state first," said Wang Xiang, chief designer of the Chinese lunar exploration program, in the English captions of a CCTV report , China's state-run broadcaster. The split cuts to the heart of a heated new space race and reveals two different institutional cultures. China's tight-lipped, military-run program trusts machines to prove its lunar hardware works. NASA's civilian program, working in public view to land astronauts first in 2028, leverages human test pilots. U.S. leaders say they're reviving the Apollo playbook that beat the Soviet Union to the moon: put crews on key test flights, launch often, and build on each mission . title: European Commission advises TikTok to redesign FYP or risk fines
body: European regulators warn TikTok 's "rabbit hole"-inducing FYP might be breaking EU law. Preliminary findings from an investigation by the European Commission accuse the social media giant of failing to mitigate the potential mental health risks of its personalized algorithmic feed in violation of the Digital Services Act. In particular, the regulatory body takes issue with the platform's "continuous stream of personalized videos" and the ways in which its algorithm determines user interest. Repeated interaction with triggering content, the report says, is interpreted as positive interest, leading to a "rabbit hole effect." SEE ALSO: A teen used her school Chromebook and Google AI Mode to plan her suicide, lawsuit alleges "This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image," the Commission writes. "These rabbit holes' can have a detrimental impact on users' mental health, especially that of vulnerable adults and minors." The early findings urged TikTok redesign its For Your Page. "TikTok should rely more on users' explicit preferences, disable viewing time as an indicator to recommend content, increase the accessibility and usability of user controls, and regularly test its algorithm," advise regulators. If TikTok fails to comply with the commission's final report and recommendations, the company may be fined up to 6 percent of its global revenue. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new. That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. title: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
author: Katarina Zimmer, Knowable Magazine
body: It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters. At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors. Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads. Read full article Comments

title: DJI unveils an all-weather drone built for pitch-black rescue missions: Features, night vision, and thermal imaging
body: TL;DR: DJI launched the Matrice 5T , a rugged enterprise drone packing 1K thermal imaging, LiDAR, and AI object tracking to find missing people in pitch-black darkness and bad weather. Opens in a new window Credit: DJI DJI Matrice 5T Learn More at DJI Searching for a missing person across dense forests or choppy waters is grueling enough in broad daylight. Once night falls, or when heavy fog and blinding rain set in, standard aerial cameras hit a hard physical wall. Search and rescue crews are often left squinting at pixelated monitor screens and hoping a flashlight beam catches something reflective. DJI designed the Matrice 5T to tackle those exact conditions. Built for first responders, disaster relief crews, and infrastructure inspectors, the enterprise drone functions as an all-in-one sensor rig engineered to handle pitch-black darkness, dense dust, and stormy weather. Instead of using a standard night camera, the Matrice 5T packs a dedicated multi-sensor setup. The heart of its nighttime search gear is a native 1K thermal camera (1280 x 1024 resolution) with four times as many pixels as typical 640 x 512 sensors, letting teams spot faint heat signatures in cold terrain or rubble. With Ultra-High Resolution mode turned on, it doubles to 2560 x 2048 to keep heat sources crisp against messy backgrounds. Thermal tech built for darkness That thermal view is backed by long-range zoom and full-color night optics. title: AI agents may run your household. What could go wrong?
body: Erica Layer, a mom of a 2- and 6-year-old, has an enviable to-do list for her AI agent. The busy executive relies on an Instinct agent for low-stakes but time-intensive household tasks like meal planning, calendaring, and birthday reminders. "I do get a huge amount of time back," Layer says of delegating to an AI agent. "But also I'm doing the things that I just was dropping completely before." Still, Layer is conflicted about her agent's persistence. The AI has suggested completing tasks on her behalf without explaining what happens to the data it accesses. Recently, her Instinct agent researched a family trip in Portugal, where she lives, and offered to book train tickets. SEE ALSO: 'Not everything needs to be known': How one day with no phone changed my life The catch? It wanted her kids' passports to make the purchase. Layer runs a fractional AI company , operates her own team of agents professionally, and has taught nearly 100 people to build agentic operating systems. She consulted Instinct's data privacy terms, felt they lacked transparency, and worried about how her data would be used. Layer, who wrote about her experience , made the reservation herself instead. Mashable attempted to contact Instinct's founder for comment but did not receive a reply as of publication. Like many parents particularly moms Layer is eager for an agent to handle the exhausting aspects of running a household. Her no-nonsense insights don't always land, however. "I get yelled at all the time," she tells Mashable in an interview. "I get yelled at for saying 'Someone texting you or someone not texting you doesn't mean they don't like you.' And people lose their marbles because it's safer to hold on to a narrative they believe than to create something new because it takes more bandwidth."
